feedback: If a learner calls dissolving irreversible because the solution looks different, respond: 'Appearance changed, but evaporating recovers the solid, so it is reversible — judge by substance, not looks.'
If a learner calls melting irreversible because heat was used, line it up against toasting: 'Both used heat; only toasting made a new substance.'
Reward justifications that name the recovery action and the 'no new substance' test rather than just the label.
activities.intendedInsight: Reversibility is judged by whether a new substance was made and the original can be recovered — not by whether heat was added or whether the material looks different.
learnerActions: Categorise a set of changes as reversible or irreversible.
Match each reversible change to the specific action that would reverse it.
For each judgement, state the reason: can the original material be recovered, with no new substance made?
Tackle tricky cases: is dissolving salt reversible even though the water looks completely different? Is re-set chocolate the same substance?
activities.title: Sort and justify: reversible or not?

feedback: If a learner predicts 'no' because heating spoils it, contrast melting ice (heated, reversible) with toasting (heated, irreversible) to move them off 'heat' and onto 'was a new substance made?'.
If a learner judges by appearance, use dissolving as the bridge: it looks totally different yet is reversible by evaporation.
Confirm a strong answer: ice↔water is reversible (same water, just a change of state); bread→toast is irreversible (a new substance forms).
activities.intendedInsight: Stating the reason before observing surfaces whether a learner is reasoning from 'heating spoils it' or appearance versus the correct test of whether a new substance was made.
learnerActions: Before any melting, predict: if we melt this chocolate in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back — and WHY?
State your reason out loud before observing (this reasoning is the important part).
Melt the chocolate, then let it set, and compare your prediction with what happened.

Answer probe questions: Is dissolving salt reversible even though it looks nothing like before? Would un-heating toast make it bread again, and why not? Then give your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain with chocolate
